Terminal p.d. V = E − Ir on discharge, E + Ir on charging; maximum power transfer when R = r

Wheatstone balance P/Q = R/S; meter bridge X/R = l/(100 − l); potentiometer E₁/E₂ = l₁/l₂

Seebeck: emf from two junctions at different temperatures; Peltier: reversible heat at a junction; T_inversion = 2T_neutral − T_cold

questions.q: If the distance between two point charges is halved, the force between them becomes
questions.x: Coulomb's law: F ∝ 1/r². Halving r gives (1/2)⁻² = 4 times the force.

questions.q: The electric field inside a charged hollow conducting sphere is
o: Equal to that at the surface
Inversely proportional to distance from the centre
questions.x: All the charge resides on the outer surface. By Gauss's law, no charge is enclosed inside, so E = 0 and the potential is constant.
questions.s: Electric field strength, potential and potential energy

questions.q: The electric potential at 9 cm from a point charge of 1 nC is (1/4πε₀ = 9 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻²)
questions.trap: 1111 V comes from using r², the electric field formula.

questions.q: Three capacitors of 6 μF each are connected in series. The equivalent capacitance is
questions.x: Series: 1/C = 1/6 + 1/6 + 1/6 = 1/2, so C = 2 μF. In parallel it would be 18 μF.
questions.trap: 18 μF adds them directly, the parallel rule for capacitors.

questions.q: The energy stored in a 10 μF capacitor charged to 100 V is
questions.trap: 0.1 J forgets the ½.

questions.q: A wire of resistance R is stretched uniformly to twice its length. Its new resistance is
questions.x: Volume stays constant, so length ×2 and area ÷2. R = ρL/A becomes ρ(2L)/(A/2) = 4R.
questions.trap: 2R forgets that the cross-section also decreases.

questions.q: Resistors of 2 Ω, 3 Ω and 6 Ω are connected in parallel. The equivalent resistance is
A cell of emf 2 V and internal resistance 0.5 Ω is connected to a 3.5 Ω resistor. The terminal potential difference is
questions.trap: 2 V: terminal voltage equals emf only when no current flows.

questions.q: Kirchhoff's junction (current) law is based on the conservation of
questions.x: Charge cannot pile up at a junction, so current in = current out. The loop (voltage) law comes from energy conservation.
questions.trap: Energy is the basis of the loop law, not the junction law.

questions.q: The resistance of the filament of a 100 W, 220 V bulb is
A charged particle moves parallel to a uniform magnetic field. The magnetic force on it is
questions.x: F = qvB sinθ; with θ = 0°, sinθ = 0, so there is no force and the particle moves undeflected.

questions.q: The magnetic field at the centre of a circular coil carrying a current is B. If the radius is doubled, keeping current and turns the same, the field becomes
questions.x: B = μ₀NI/2r, so B ∝ 1/r; doubling r halves B.
questions.trap: B/4 wrongly uses the 1/r² dependence of a point charge's field.

questions.q: A proton and an alpha particle enter a uniform magnetic field at right angles with the same speed. The ratio of the radius of the alpha particle's path to that of the proton is
questions.x: r = mv/qB ∝ m/q. Proton: m/e; alpha: 4m/2e = 2(m/e). So r_α : r_p = 2 : 1.
questions.trap: 4 : 1 uses the mass ratio and forgets the alpha's charge is 2e.

questions.q: Lenz's law is a consequence of the conservation of
questions.x: The induced current opposes the change causing it, so work must be done to produce it. Otherwise energy would be created from nothing.

questions.q: A transformer has 100 turns in the primary and 500 turns in the secondary. If the primary voltage is 220 V AC, the secondary voltage is
questions.x: Vs/Vp = Ns/Np, so Vs = 220 × 500/100 = 1100 V (step-up).
questions.trap: 44 V comes from inverting the turns ratio.

questions.q: In an AC circuit containing only a pure inductor, the current
o: Is in phase with the voltage
questions.x: For a pure inductor V = L dI/dt, so current lags voltage by π/2 and the power factor is zero.
questions.trap: 'Leads by 90°' is true for a pure capacitor.

questions.q: In the photoelectric effect, the maximum kinetic energy of emitted electrons depends on
o: The area of the metal surface
questions.x: KE_max = hν − φ. Intensity changes only the number of electrons emitted (photocurrent), not their maximum energy.
questions.trap: Intensity raises the photocurrent, not the electron energy.

questions.q: Light with photon energy 5 eV falls on a metal of work function 2 eV. The stopping potential is
questions.x: eV₀ = hν − φ = 5 − 2 = 3 eV, so V₀ = 3 V.

questions.q: The energy of the electron in the second orbit (n = 2) of a hydrogen atom is
questions.trap: −6.8 eV divides by n instead of n².

questions.q: The longest-wavelength line of the Balmer series of hydrogen is due to the electron transition
questions.x: Balmer lines end on n = 2. Longest wavelength means smallest energy gap: 3 → 2. The ∞ → 2 transition gives the shortest (series limit).
questions.trap: ∞ → 2 gives the shortest Balmer wavelength, not the longest.

questions.q: An X-ray tube is operated at 12.4 kV. The minimum wavelength of the X-rays produced is (hc = 12400 eV Å)
questions.x: λ_min = hc/eV = 12400 eV Å / 12400 eV = 1.0 Å.

questions.q: A radioactive sample of 80 g has a half-life of 5 days. The mass left undecayed after 15 days is
questions.x: 15 days = 3 half-lives: 80 → 40 → 20 → 10 g.
questions.trap: 20 g stops after two halvings; 26.7 g divides by 3 instead of halving three times.

questions.q: When a nucleus emits an alpha particle, its
o: Mass number falls by 2 and atomic number by 4
Atomic number rises by 1; mass number is unchanged
Mass number falls by 4 and atomic number by 2
Mass number and atomic number are both unchanged
questions.x: An α particle is a helium nucleus (A = 4, Z = 2). β⁻ emission raises Z by 1; γ emission changes neither.

questions.q: Pure silicon doped with phosphorus (a pentavalent impurity) becomes
o: A p-type semiconductor with holes as majority carriers
An n-type semiconductor with holes as majority carriers
An n-type semiconductor with electrons as majority carriers
questions.x: Phosphorus has 5 valence electrons; the fifth becomes a free electron, so electrons are majority carriers (n-type). Trivalent B or Al gives p-type.

questions.q: The output of a NOR gate is 1 (high) only when
questions.x: NOR = NOT(A + B). A + B = 0 only when A = B = 0, so the output is 1 only then.
questions.trap: 'Both inputs 1' describes when AND gives 1.

questions.q: Which of these charges can NOT exist on an isolated body? (e = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C)
questions.x: Charge is quantised: q = ne with n a whole number. 2.4 × 10⁻¹⁹/1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ = 1.5, not an integer. The others are 2e, 3e and 10e.

questions.q: A glass rod rubbed with silk becomes positively charged because it
questions.x: Only electrons move during rubbing; protons are bound in nuclei. Glass gives up electrons, so it is left positive and the silk becomes negative.
questions.trap: Protons never transfer by rubbing; only electrons do.

questions.q: Two point charges exert a force F on each other in air. If they are placed at the same separation in a medium of dielectric constant 4, the force becomes
questions.x: In a medium F = q₁q₂/(4πε₀K r²), so the force falls by the factor K = 4.

questions.q: A positively charged rod is brought near (not touching) a neutral, insulated metal sphere. The sphere is
o: Not affected, since it is neutral
Attracted only if it is earthed
questions.x: Induction puts negative charge on the near side and positive on the far side. The nearer negative charge feels a stronger pull, so there is a net attraction.
questions.trap: A neutral body still feels a force because induced charges are at different distances.

questions.q: The electric field at 3 m from a point charge of 2 μC is (1/4πε₀ = 9 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻²)
questions.trap: 6000 N C⁻¹ divides by r instead of r², which gives potential-like scaling.

questions.q: Charges +4 μC and +1 μC are 3 cm apart. The electric field is zero at a point on the line joining them
o: Beyond the +1 μC charge, outside the pair
questions.x: Between like charges: 4/x² = 1/(3 − x)², so 2(3 − x) = x and x = 2 cm from the larger charge. The null point is nearer the smaller charge.
questions.trap: 1 cm puts the null point near the larger charge; it lies nearer the smaller one.

questions.q: The SI unit N C⁻¹ of electric field is equivalent to
questions.x: E = V/d, so N C⁻¹ = V m⁻¹. J C⁻¹ is the volt, the unit of potential.

questions.s: Electric field strength, potential and potential energy
questions.q: Which of the following is a vector quantity?
questions.x: Electric field has magnitude and direction and adds by vector rules. Current has a direction along the wire but adds as a scalar.
questions.trap: Current has direction but does not obey vector addition, so it is a scalar.

questions.s: Electric field strength, potential and potential energy
questions.q: At a large distance r from a short electric dipole, the electric potential varies as
questions.x: Dipole potential V = kp cosθ/r², so V ∝ 1/r². Its field falls faster, as 1/r³.
questions.trap: 1/r is for a single point charge.

questions.s: Electric field strength, potential and potential energy
questions.q: At a large distance r from a short electric dipole, the electric field varies as
questions.x: E = −dV/dr and V ∝ 1/r², so E ∝ 1/r³ (both on the axis and on the equator).
questions.trap: 1/r² is the dipole potential, not its field.

questions.s: Electric field strength, potential and potential energy
questions.q: By Gauss's law, the total electric flux through a closed surface enclosing a charge q is
questions.x: Gauss's law: ∮E·dA = q_enclosed/ε₀. It is zero only when the net enclosed charge is zero.

questions.s: Electric field strength, potential and potential energy
questions.q: A point charge q is placed at the centre of a cube. The electric flux through one face of the cube is
questions.x: Total flux q/ε₀ is shared equally by the six symmetric faces: q/6ε₀ each.
questions.trap: q/ε₀ is the flux through the whole cube.

questions.s: Electric field strength, potential and potential energy
questions.q: The work done in moving a charge between two points on an equipotential surface is
questions.x: W = qΔV and ΔV = 0 on an equipotential surface, so W = 0. Field lines cross equipotentials at right angles.

questions.s: Electric field strength, potential and potential energy
questions.q: The electrostatic potential energy of two charges of +1 μC each kept 10 cm apart in air is (k = 9 × 10⁹ SI units)
questions.trap: 0.9 J forgets to convert 10 cm into 0.1 m correctly.

questions.s: Electric field strength, potential and potential energy
questions.q: A proton starting from rest is accelerated through a potential difference of 1 V. Its kinetic energy becomes
questions.x: KE = qV = e × 1 V = 1 eV = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ J. The gain depends on charge, not mass, so an electron would also get 1 eV.
questions.trap: 1836 eV wrongly scales the energy with the proton's mass.

questions.s: Electric field strength, potential and potential energy
questions.q: A potential difference of 200 V is applied across two parallel plates 2 mm apart. The electric field between them is
questions.x: Uniform field E = V/d = 200/(2 × 10⁻³) = 1 × 10⁵ V m⁻¹.
questions.trap: 400 V m⁻¹ multiplies V by d instead of dividing.

questions.s: Electric field strength, potential and potential energy
questions.q: Inside a charged hollow conducting sphere, the electric potential is
o: Constant and equal to the potential at the surface
questions.x: E = 0 inside, and E = −dV/dr, so V does not change: it stays at the surface value kQ/R.
questions.trap: Zero field does not mean zero potential; it means constant potential.

questions.q: If the separation between the plates of a parallel plate capacitor is doubled, its capacitance becomes
questions.x: C = ε₀A/d, so C ∝ 1/d. Doubling d halves C.

questions.q: The space between the plates of a capacitor of capacitance C is completely filled with a dielectric of dielectric constant K. The new capacitance is
questions.x: C = Kε₀A/d; the dielectric multiplies capacitance by K.

questions.q: A capacitor is charged and then disconnected from the battery. A dielectric slab of K = 2 is then inserted to fill the gap. The energy stored
questions.x: Charge Q stays fixed when isolated. C doubles, so U = Q²/2C halves (V also halves).
questions.trap: Doubling is the result when the battery stays connected (V fixed).

questions.q: Four identical capacitors are connected first to give the maximum and then the minimum possible capacitance. The ratio C_max : C_min is
questions.x: All parallel: 4C. All series: C/4. Ratio = 4C/(C/4) = 16 = n².
questions.trap: 4 : 1 compares the parallel value with a single capacitor only.

questions.q: Capacitors of 2 μF and 3 μF are connected in parallel across a 10 V supply. The total charge drawn from the supply is
questions.x: Parallel: C = 2 + 3 = 5 μF; Q = CV = 5 × 10 = 50 μC.
questions.trap: 12 μC uses the series value 1.2 μF.

questions.q: The energy stored per unit volume in an electric field E in vacuum is
questions.x: u = U/(Ad) = ½CV²/(Ad) = ½(ε₀A/d)(Ed)²/(Ad) = ½ε₀E².

questions.q: One farad is equal to
questions.x: C = Q/V, so 1 F = 1 C V⁻¹. J C⁻¹ is the volt.

questions.q: A 4 μF capacitor charged to 50 V is connected across an identical uncharged 4 μF capacitor. The fraction of the original stored energy lost is
questions.x: Initial U = ½ × 4μ × 50² = 5 mJ. Common V = 25 V; final U = ½ × 8μ × 25² = 2.5 mJ. Half is lost as heat and radiation.
questions.trap: Zero assumes charge sharing conserves energy; only charge is conserved.

questions.q: The current I in a conductor is related to the drift velocity v_d of free electrons by (n = electron density, A = area)
questions.x: Charge crossing a section per second = (number per volume) × (volume swept per second) × e = n(Av_d)e.

questions.q: A steady current flows through a wire whose cross-section is not uniform. The drift speed of electrons is greatest where the wire is
questions.x: Current is the same at every section, so v_d = I/(neA) ∝ 1/A: smallest area, largest drift speed.
questions.trap: Students assume drift speed is uniform because the current is.

questions.q: Which of the following does NOT obey Ohm's law?
o: A copper wire at constant temperature
A nichrome wire at constant temperature
questions.x: A diode's I–V graph is non-linear and depends on bias direction. Metallic conductors at constant temperature are ohmic.

questions.q: A wire is cut and its length halved. Its resistivity
questions.x: Resistivity depends only on the material and temperature. Resistance halves (R = ρL/A), resistivity does not.
questions.trap: Halving confuses resistivity with resistance.

questions.q: A 1000 W heater runs for 2 hours. The electrical energy used is
questions.x: Energy = power × time = 1 kW × 2 h = 2 kWh = 2 units.

questions.q: Resistors of 2 Ω and 4 Ω are connected in series to a battery. The ratio of heat produced in them (2 Ω : 4 Ω) is
questions.x: In series the same current flows, so H = I²Rt ∝ R: 2 : 4 = 1 : 2.
questions.trap: 2 : 1 is the parallel answer, where H ∝ 1/R.

questions.q: Resistors of 2 Ω and 4 Ω are connected in parallel across a battery. The ratio of heat produced in them (2 Ω : 4 Ω) is
questions.x: In parallel the voltage is the same, so H = V²t/R ∝ 1/R: (1/2) : (1/4) = 2 : 1.
questions.trap: 1 : 2 is the series answer, where H ∝ R.

questions.q: A 100 W and a 60 W bulb, both rated 220 V, are connected in series across 220 V. Which glows brighter?
questions.x: R = V²/P, so the 60 W bulb has higher resistance. In series the current is common, so P = I²R is larger for the 60 W bulb.
questions.trap: The 100 W bulb is brighter only when connected in parallel.

questions.q: As the temperature of a pure semiconductor rises, its resistance
questions.x: Heat frees more electron–hole pairs, so conductivity rises (negative temperature coefficient). Metals show the opposite.
questions.trap: 'Increases' is true for metals, not semiconductors.

questions.q: A cell of internal resistance r delivers maximum power to an external resistor R when
questions.x: Maximum power transfer theorem: P = E²R/(R + r)² is greatest when R = r.

questions.q: A current of 2 A flows through a 5 Ω resistor. The power dissipated is
questions.x: P = I²R = 2² × 5 = 20 W.
questions.trap: 10 W uses P = IR, which is a voltage, not power.

questions.q: While a cell of emf E and internal resistance r is being charged by a current I, its terminal voltage is
questions.x: During charging, current enters the positive terminal, so the charger must supply E plus the drop across r: V = E + Ir.
questions.trap: E − Ir applies when the cell is discharging.

questions.q: A uniform wire of resistance 12 Ω is bent into a circle. The resistance between two diametrically opposite points is
questions.x: Each half is 6 Ω and the two halves are in parallel: 6 × 6/(6 + 6) = 3 Ω.
questions.trap: 6 Ω takes only one half and forgets the parallel path.

questions.q: Three 3 Ω resistors are all used together in some combination. Which equivalent resistance is NOT possible?
questions.x: All parallel 1 Ω; two series in parallel with one: 6 × 3/9 = 2 Ω; two parallel in series with one: 1.5 + 3 = 4.5 Ω; all series 9 Ω. 3 Ω cannot be made.

questions.q: Kirchhoff's loop (voltage) law is a statement of the conservation of
questions.x: Around a closed loop the sum of emfs equals the sum of IR drops, i.e. the net work on a charge round the loop is zero.
questions.trap: Charge conservation is the junction law.

questions.q: In a balanced Wheatstone bridge, P = 10 Ω, Q = 20 Ω and R = 15 Ω. The fourth resistance S is
questions.x: Balance: P/Q = R/S, so S = RQ/P = 15 × 20/10 = 30 Ω.
questions.trap: 7.5 Ω inverts the ratio.

questions.q: The balance of a Wheatstone bridge is NOT disturbed by changing
o: The resistance in one ratio arm
questions.x: The balance condition P/Q = R/S contains only the four arm resistances; the cell emf (and galvanometer) do not appear.

questions.q: In a meter bridge, an unknown resistance X is in the left gap and 6 Ω is in the right gap. The null point is 40 cm from the left end. X is
questions.trap: 9 Ω uses 60/40, putting the lengths the wrong way round.

questions.q: A potentiometer is preferred to a voltmeter for measuring the emf of a cell because at balance it
o: Draws maximum current from the cell
Draws no current from the cell
questions.x: At the null point no current flows from the cell, so there is no Ir drop and the true emf is measured.

questions.q: On a potentiometer, a cell of emf 1.5 V balances at 60 cm. Another cell balances at 80 cm on the same wire. Its emf is
questions.x: E₁/E₂ = l₁/l₂, so E₂ = 1.5 × 80/60 = 2.0 V.
questions.trap: 1.125 V uses 60/80, the inverse ratio.

questions.q: A galvanometer is converted into an ammeter by connecting
o: A low resistance in parallel with it
A high resistance in series with it
A low resistance in series with it
A high resistance in parallel with it
questions.x: A small shunt in parallel carries most of the current, protecting the galvanometer and lowering total resistance.
questions.trap: A high series resistance makes a voltmeter, not an ammeter.

questions.q: A galvanometer of resistance 100 Ω gives full-scale deflection for 1 mA. To use it as a voltmeter of range 10 V, the resistance needed in series is
questions.trap: 10000 Ω forgets to subtract the galvanometer's own 100 Ω.

questions.q: A galvanometer of resistance 99 Ω is to be converted into an ammeter that reads 100 times its full-scale current. The shunt required is
questions.trap: 0.99 Ω uses G/n instead of G/(n − 1).

questions.q: The resistance of an ideal voltmeter is
questions.x: An ideal voltmeter draws no current from the circuit, so its resistance must be infinite. An ideal ammeter has zero resistance.

questions.q: The production of an emf in a circuit of two dissimilar metals whose junctions are kept at different temperatures is called the
questions.x: Seebeck effect: temperature difference → emf (the thermocouple principle). Peltier is the reverse: current → heat at a junction.

questions.q: When a current passes through the junction of two dissimilar metals, heat is absorbed or released at the junction. This is the
questions.x: Peltier effect: heating or cooling at a junction depending on current direction.
questions.trap: Joule heating occurs throughout the wire, not just at the junction.

questions.q: Compared with Joule heating, the Peltier effect is
o: Proportional to the square of the current
Present throughout the whole length of the wire
Reversible: reversing the current turns heating into cooling
questions.x: Peltier heat ∝ I and changes sign with current direction. Joule heat ∝ I²R and is always produced, so it is irreversible.
questions.trap: I² dependence belongs to Joule heating.

questions.q: For a thermocouple with the cold junction at 0 °C, the neutral temperature is 270 °C. The temperature of inversion is
questions.x: Neutral temperature lies midway: T_n = (T_c + T_i)/2, so T_i = 2 × 270 − 0 = 540 °C.
questions.trap: 270 °C is the neutral temperature, where the emf is maximum.

questions.q: The rms value of the household AC supply is 220 V. Its peak value is about
questions.trap: 156 V divides by √2 instead of multiplying.

questions.q: For a sinusoidal alternating current, the ratio of its mean value over a half-cycle to its rms value is
questions.x: Mean = 2I₀/π, rms = I₀/√2. Ratio = (2I₀/π)/(I₀/√2) = 2√2/π ≈ 0.90.
questions.trap: π/2√2 is the inverse ratio (rms/mean).

questions.q: In a series RC circuit connected to an AC source, the current
o: Lags the voltage by an angle between 0° and 90°
Is in phase with the voltage
Leads the voltage by an angle between 0° and 90°
questions.x: tanφ = X_C/R. With some resistance the lead is less than 90°; exactly 90° needs a pure capacitor.
questions.trap: Lagging current means an inductive (RL) circuit.

questions.q: In a steady DC circuit, a fully charged capacitor behaves as
questions.x: X_C = 1/(2πfC) is infinite for f = 0, so no steady current flows through it.

questions.q: At resonance in a series LCR circuit
o: The impedance is minimum and equal to R
The voltage leads the current by 90°
questions.x: At f₀ = 1/(2π√LC), X_L = X_C cancel, so Z = R, current is maximum and power factor is 1.
questions.trap: Maximum impedance at resonance is for a parallel LC circuit.

questions.q: A series circuit has R = 30 Ω and net reactance 40 Ω. Its power factor is
questions.trap: 0.8 uses X/Z instead of R/Z.

questions.q: The average power consumed over a full cycle by a pure inductor connected to an AC source is
questions.x: Phase difference 90° gives power factor cos 90° = 0. Energy stored in one quarter-cycle is returned in the next (wattless current).

questions.q: The Q-factor of a series LCR circuit increases when
questions.x: Q = (1/R)√(L/C). Smaller R or larger L raises Q; larger C lowers it. High Q means a sharper resonance.

questions.q: A full-wave bridge rectifier uses
questions.x: The bridge has four diodes; two conduct in each half-cycle. A centre-tap full-wave rectifier uses two, a half-wave rectifier one.
questions.trap: Two diodes is the centre-tapped type, not the bridge.

questions.q: A full-wave rectifier is fed with 50 Hz AC. The fundamental frequency of the output ripple is
questions.x: Both half-cycles give an output pulse, so there are 2 × 50 = 100 pulses per second.
questions.trap: 50 Hz is the half-wave rectifier output.

questions.q: The reactance of a 0.1 H inductor at 50 Hz is about
questions.trap: 5 Ω forgets the 2π.

questions.q: Permanent magnets are made of steel rather than soft iron because steel has
questions.x: A permanent magnet must keep its magnetism (retentivity) and resist demagnetisation (coercivity); steel's wide hysteresis loop gives both.
questions.trap: Low coercivity suits electromagnets, which must lose magnetism easily.

questions.q: Soft iron is preferred for the core of a transformer or electromagnet because it has
questions.x: Soft iron magnetises and demagnetises easily with a thin hysteresis loop, so energy loss per cycle is small.

questions.q: A diamagnetic substance has a magnetic susceptibility that is
questions.x: Diamagnets are weakly repelled by a magnet: χ is small and negative and μ_r is slightly less than 1.
questions.trap: Small and positive describes paramagnets.

questions.q: According to Curie's law, the susceptibility of a paramagnetic substance is
o: Directly proportional to its absolute temperature
Inversely proportional to its absolute temperature
questions.x: χ = C/T: heat disorders the atomic dipoles, so alignment and χ fall as T rises.

questions.q: When a ferromagnetic material is heated above its Curie temperature, it becomes
questions.x: Thermal agitation destroys the domain alignment above the Curie point; the material then behaves as a paramagnet.

questions.q: The area enclosed by the hysteresis loop of a ferromagnetic material represents
o: Energy lost per unit volume per cycle of magnetisation
questions.x: Loop area = heat lost per unit volume per cycle. Retentivity and coercivity are intercepts on the axes, not the area.

questions.q: Which of the following is diamagnetic?
questions.x: Bismuth (also copper, water) is diamagnetic. Aluminium is paramagnetic; iron and nickel are ferromagnetic.

questions.q: A long straight wire carries a current of 10 A. The magnetic field at 10 cm from it is (μ₀ = 4π × 10⁻⁷ T m A⁻¹)
questions.x: B = μ₀I/(2πr) = 4π × 10⁻⁷ × 10/(2π × 0.1) = 2 × 10⁻⁵ T. Field lines are circles around the wire.
questions.trap: 6.28 × 10⁻⁵ T uses the coil-centre formula μ₀I/2r.

questions.q: The number of turns per unit length of a long solenoid and the current in it are both doubled. The magnetic field inside becomes
questions.x: B = μ₀nI, so doubling n and I gives 2 × 2 = 4 times the field.

questions.q: The magnetic field inside a long current-carrying solenoid is
questions.x: Inside an ideal long solenoid B = μ₀nI, uniform and parallel to the axis; outside it is nearly zero.

questions.q: Two long parallel wires carry currents in the same direction. They
o: Exert no force on each other
questions.x: Each wire sits in the other's field; F = BIL gives attraction for like currents and repulsion for opposite currents.
questions.trap: Students carry over 'like charges repel' to currents; like currents attract.

questions.q: A 10 cm wire carrying 2 A lies perpendicular to a uniform magnetic field of 0.5 T. The force on it is
questions.trap: 1 N leaves the length in centimetres.

questions.q: The magnetic force on a moving charged particle does no work because
o: The force is always parallel to the velocity
The force is always perpendicular to the velocity
The force is zero for a moving charge
questions.x: F = qv × B is perpendicular to v, so F·v = 0: speed and kinetic energy stay constant; only direction changes.

questions.q: A charged particle moves in a circle in a uniform magnetic field. Its time period does NOT depend on its
questions.x: T = 2πr/v and r = mv/qB give T = 2πm/qB: faster particles move in bigger circles in the same time (the cyclotron principle).
questions.trap: Radius depends on speed, but the period does not.

questions.q: The Hall effect in a current-carrying slab placed in a magnetic field is used to find
o: The resistivity of the slab only
The sign and number density of the charge carriers
questions.x: The sign of the Hall voltage shows whether carriers are electrons or holes; V_H = BI/(nqt) gives the carrier density n.

questions.q: In the Hall effect, the Hall voltage develops in a direction
o: Perpendicular to both the current and the magnetic field
questions.x: The magnetic force qv × B pushes carriers sideways, perpendicular to both I and B, building a transverse voltage.

questions.q: The torque on a current-carrying rectangular coil in a uniform magnetic field is maximum when the plane of the coil is
questions.x: τ = NIAB sinθ, θ between the coil's normal and B. Plane parallel to B means θ = 90°, so torque is maximum.
questions.trap: Perpendicular plane gives θ = 0° and zero torque.

questions.q: The SI unit of magnetic flux is the
questions.x: Φ = BA, so the unit is T m² = weber (Wb). Tesla is the unit of flux density B.
questions.trap: Tesla measures B, not flux.

questions.q: The flux through a 10-turn coil changes from 0.5 Wb to 0.1 Wb in 0.2 s. The average induced emf is
questions.trap: 2 V forgets to multiply by the 10 turns.

questions.q: The henry, the SI unit of self-inductance, is equivalent to
questions.x: L = Φ/I, so 1 H = 1 Wb A⁻¹ = 1 V s A⁻¹ = 1 Ω s.

questions.q: The energy stored in an inductor of 2 H carrying a current of 3 A is
questions.x: U = ½LI² = ½ × 2 × 3² = 9 J.
questions.trap: 18 J forgets the ½.

questions.q: The current in a 0.5 H coil changes steadily by 4 A in 0.1 s. The self-induced emf is
questions.trap: 2 V forgets to divide by the time 0.1 s.

questions.q: The core of a transformer is laminated in order to reduce
questions.x: Thin insulated sheets break up the large loops of eddy currents induced in the core. Soft iron (not lamination) reduces hysteresis loss.
questions.trap: Hysteresis loss is cut by choosing soft iron, not by laminating.

questions.q: In an AC generator, the induced emf is maximum when the plane of the rotating coil is
o: At any angle, since emf is constant
questions.x: ε = NBAω sinωt. When the plane is parallel to B the flux is zero but changing fastest, so emf is maximum.
questions.trap: Perpendicular plane has maximum flux but zero rate of change.

questions.q: A 100-turn coil of area 0.01 m² rotates at 100 rad s⁻¹ in a uniform field of 0.1 T. The peak emf is
In an ideal step-up transformer, compared with the primary current, the secondary current is
questions.x: Power is conserved: V_pI_p = V_sI_s. Raising the voltage lowers the current in the same ratio.
questions.trap: Students assume 'step-up' raises everything, current included.

questions.q: The mutual inductance of a pair of coils does NOT depend on
o: The number of turns in the coils
The current flowing in the coils
questions.x: M depends only on geometry (turns, area, separation, orientation) and the core's permeability, not on the current.

questions.q: The ratio of the radii of the nuclei ²⁷Al and ⁶⁴Cu is
questions.trap: 27 : 64 forgets the cube root.

questions.q: The ratio of the nuclear densities of ⁵⁶Fe and ²³⁸U is about
questions.x: R³ ∝ A, so volume ∝ A and density = mass/volume ∝ A/A: all nuclei have nearly the same density.
questions.trap: Students assume a heavier nucleus is denser.

questions.q: The density of nuclear matter is of the order of
questions.x: About 2.3 × 10¹⁷ kg m⁻³, the same for all nuclei, since nuclear volume is proportional to mass number.

questions.q: The energy equivalent of 1 atomic mass unit (1 u) is about
questions.x: E = mc² for 1.66 × 10⁻²⁷ kg gives 931.5 MeV. 0.511 MeV is the rest energy of an electron.

questions.q: The mass defect of a nucleus is 0.1 u. Its binding energy is about
The binding energy per nucleon is maximum for nuclei near
questions.x: The curve peaks near iron (about 8.8 MeV per nucleon). Heavy nuclei gain stability by fission, light ones by fusion.
questions.trap: ²³⁸U has the largest total binding energy, not the largest per nucleon.

questions.q: If 1 g of matter were completely converted into energy, the energy released would be (c = 3 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹)
questions.trap: 9 × 10¹⁶ J uses 1 kg instead of 1 g.

questions.q: The energy released in the fission of one ²³⁵U nucleus is about
questions.x: A slow neutron splits ²³⁵U into two medium nuclei plus 2–3 neutrons, releasing about 200 MeV.

questions.q: The main source of the Sun's energy is
o: Nuclear fusion of hydrogen into helium
questions.x: In the core, hydrogen nuclei fuse into helium; the mass defect appears as energy.

questions.q: Nuclear fusion requires temperatures of millions of kelvin because
o: The nuclei must first be ionised into electrons
The nuclei must overcome their electrostatic repulsion
questions.x: Positive nuclei repel; only very high kinetic energy lets them come within range of the short-range nuclear force.

questions.q: In a nuclear reactor, cadmium or boron rods are used to
o: Slow down neutrons as a moderator
Absorb neutrons and control the chain reaction
questions.x: Control rods absorb neutrons. Moderators such as heavy water or graphite slow neutrons without absorbing them.
questions.trap: Slowing neutrons is the moderator's job, not the control rods'.

questions.q: The force that holds nucleons together in a nucleus is
o: Short-range and nearly independent of charge
questions.x: The strong nuclear force acts only within about 2–3 fm and is the same for p–p, n–n and p–n pairs.

questions.q: Millikan's oil drop experiment established
o: The specific charge e/m of the electron
That charge is quantised and measured the electronic charge
The wave nature of the electron
questions.x: Charges on oil drops were always whole multiples of 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C. Thomson measured e/m; Rutherford found the nucleus.
questions.trap: e/m was measured by J.J. Thomson, not Millikan.

questions.q: J.J. Thomson's experiment with crossed electric and magnetic fields measured the electron's
questions.x: Balancing fields gave the speed (v = E/B), and deflection then gave e/m ≈ 1.76 × 10¹¹ C kg⁻¹.

questions.q: An electron passes undeflected through crossed fields E = 3 × 10⁴ V m⁻¹ and B = 0.01 T. Its speed is
questions.x: No deflection when eE = evB, so v = E/B = 3 × 10⁴/0.01 = 3 × 10⁶ m s⁻¹.
questions.trap: 3 × 10² multiplies E by B instead of dividing.

questions.q: The specific charge (e/m) of an electron is about
questions.x: e/m = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹/9.1 × 10⁻³¹ ≈ 1.76 × 10¹¹ C kg⁻¹. 9.58 × 10⁷ C kg⁻¹ is the proton's value.

questions.q: An oil drop of mass 3.2 × 10⁻¹⁵ kg stays stationary between plates where E = 2 × 10⁵ V m⁻¹. The number of excess electrons on it is (g = 10 m s⁻², e = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C)
An electron enters a uniform electric field at right angles to the field lines. Its path inside the field is a
questions.x: Constant force along the field and constant velocity across it give a parabola, like a horizontal projectile. A magnetic field gives a circle.
questions.trap: A circle is the path in a perpendicular magnetic field.

questions.q: In the photoelectric effect, the saturation photocurrent depends on the
questions.x: More intense light delivers more photons per second, ejecting more electrons; saturation current ∝ intensity (above threshold).
questions.trap: Frequency controls electron energy, not the number of electrons.

questions.q: The rest mass of a photon is
questions.x: A photon always moves at c and has no rest mass. Its momentum is h/λ and its energy hν.
questions.trap: hν/c² is an effective mass in motion, not rest mass.

questions.q: The work function of a metal is 2 eV. Its threshold wavelength is about (hc ≈ 12400 eV Å)
questions.x: λ₀ = hc/φ = 12400/2 = 6200 Å. Longer wavelengths cannot eject electrons.
questions.trap: 24800 Å multiplies by 2 instead of dividing.

questions.q: Light of wavelength 310 nm falls on a metal of work function 2 eV. The maximum speed of the photoelectrons is about (hc = 1240 eV nm, m_e = 9.1 × 10⁻³¹ kg)
questions.trap: 1.2 × 10⁶ m s⁻¹ forgets to subtract the work function.

questions.q: The slope of the graph of stopping potential V₀ against frequency ν of incident light is
questions.x: eV₀ = hν − φ, so V₀ = (h/e)ν − φ/e: a straight line of slope h/e, the same for every metal.

questions.q: Which observation in the photoelectric effect can NOT be explained by the wave theory of light?
o: Emission of electrons from metal surfaces
Partial reflection of the light from the metal
questions.x: Wave theory predicts that any frequency would eject electrons if intense enough. A cut-off frequency needs photons of energy hν.

questions.q: The value of Planck's constant is about
questions.x: h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s; its unit J s is the same as that of angular momentum.
questions.trap: J s⁻¹ is the watt, a unit of power.

questions.q: The energy of a photon of wavelength 6200 Å is about (hc ≈ 12400 eV Å)
A lamp emits 3.3 W of light of wavelength 600 nm. The number of photons emitted per second is about (h = 6.6 × 10⁻³⁴ J s)
The de Broglie wavelength of a material particle is inversely proportional to its
questions.x: λ = h/p = h/mv. It is inversely proportional to √(KE), not to KE.
questions.trap: Kinetic energy enters as √K, not K.

questions.q: An electron and a proton have the same de Broglie wavelength. They must have the same
questions.x: λ = h/p, so equal λ means equal p. The lighter electron then moves faster and has more kinetic energy.
questions.trap: Equal wavelength does not mean equal speed; masses differ.

questions.q: An electron and a proton have equal de Broglie wavelengths. Which has the greater kinetic energy?
o: The electron, by about m_p/m_e ≈ 1836 times
questions.x: Equal λ means equal p. KE = p²/2m, so KE ∝ 1/m: the lighter electron has about 1836 times more.

questions.q: An electron is accelerated from rest through 100 V. Its de Broglie wavelength is about (λ = 12.27/√V Å)
questions.trap: 12.27 Å forgets the square root of V.

questions.q: According to the uncertainty principle, if the position of a particle is known exactly, the uncertainty in its momentum is
questions.x: Δx Δp ≥ h/4π. Δx → 0 forces Δp → ∞.

questions.q: Bohr's quantisation condition for an electron in the nth orbit is
questions.x: Only orbits where angular momentum is a whole multiple of h/2π are allowed.

questions.q: The radius of the first Bohr orbit of hydrogen is 0.53 Å. The radius of the third orbit is
questions.trap: 1.59 Å multiplies by n instead of n².

questions.q: As the principal quantum number n increases, the speed of the electron in a Bohr orbit of hydrogen
questions.x: vₙ = v₁/n (v₁ ≈ 2.2 × 10⁶ m s⁻¹). Radius grows as n², speed falls as 1/n.

questions.q: The energy needed to ionise a hydrogen atom from its first excited state (n = 2) is
questions.x: E₂ = −13.6/4 = −3.4 eV; removing the electron to E = 0 needs 3.4 eV.
questions.trap: 13.6 eV is the ionisation energy from the ground state.

questions.q: The Lyman series of hydrogen lies in the
questions.x: Lyman lines end on n = 1, the largest energy gaps, so they are UV. Balmer (n = 2) is visible; Paschen (n = 3) is infrared.

questions.q: Hydrogen atoms are excited to the n = 4 level. The maximum number of spectral lines they can emit on returning to the ground state is
questions.x: Number of lines = n(n − 1)/2 = 4 × 3/2 = 6.
questions.trap: 3 counts only the direct jumps of one atom (4→3→2→1).

questions.q: The energy of the photon emitted when a hydrogen electron falls from n = 2 to n = 1 is
questions.x: ΔE = 13.6(1 − 1/4) = 10.2 eV, the first Lyman line. 12.09 eV is the 3 → 1 transition.

questions.q: A major limitation of Bohr's atomic model is that it
o: Cannot explain the line spectrum of hydrogen
Cannot give the ionisation energy of hydrogen
Cannot explain the spectra of atoms with more than one electron
Cannot explain the stability of the hydrogen atom
questions.x: Bohr's model works only for hydrogen-like (one-electron) systems; it also fails for fine structure, line intensities and the Zeeman effect.
questions.trap: Bohr's model does explain hydrogen's spectrum and stability; that was its success.

questions.q: X-rays are produced when
o: Slow neutrons strike a light target
Fast-moving electrons are suddenly stopped by a heavy metal target
Electrons move between outer valence orbits
questions.x: In a Coolidge tube, high-energy electrons strike a target such as tungsten; their deceleration and inner-shell transitions emit X-rays.

questions.q: Increasing the accelerating voltage of an X-ray tube makes the X-rays
o: Harder: shorter minimum wavelength and more penetrating
Softer: longer wavelength and less penetrating
More intense but with the same wavelengths
questions.x: λ_min = hc/eV falls as V rises, so the X-rays carry more energy and penetrate more. Intensity is set by the filament current.
questions.trap: Intensity is controlled by the filament current, not the voltage.

questions.q: In a Coolidge X-ray tube, the intensity of the X-rays is controlled by the
questions.x: The filament current sets how many electrons are emitted and so how many X-ray photons are produced. The voltage sets their hardness.
questions.trap: The voltage controls penetrating power (quality), not quantity.

questions.q: X-rays are NOT deflected by electric or magnetic fields because they
o: Move too fast to be deflected
questions.x: X-rays are high-energy photons with no charge, so neither field exerts a force on them.

questions.q: In a Bragg reflection, the first-order maximum occurs at a glancing angle of 30° from crystal planes 2 Å apart. The X-ray wavelength is
questions.x: 2d sinθ = nλ: λ = 2 × 2 × sin30°/1 = 2 Å.
questions.trap: 1 Å forgets the factor 2 in 2d sinθ.

questions.q: Bones show up clearly in an X-ray image mainly because
o: X-rays are reflected only by soft tissue
Bone absorbs X-rays more strongly than soft tissue
questions.x: Absorption rises with atomic number and density; calcium-rich bone absorbs more, casting a light shadow on the film.

questions.q: The wave nature of electrons was first confirmed experimentally by
questions.x: Davisson and Germer observed diffraction of electrons by a nickel crystal, matching λ = h/p.

questions.q: Among α, β and γ radiations, the one with the greatest ionising power is
questions.x: Ionising power: α > β > γ. Penetrating power is the reverse: γ > β > α.
questions.trap: γ-rays penetrate most but ionise least.

questions.q: When a nucleus emits a γ-ray photon,
o: Its atomic number and mass number both stay the same
questions.x: γ emission only releases excess energy from an excited nucleus; the numbers of protons and neutrons are unchanged.

questions.q: In β⁻ decay, the particle emitted together with the electron is
questions.x: n → p + e⁻ + ν̄. The antineutrino carries off the missing energy, explaining the continuous β spectrum. β⁺ decay emits a neutrino.
questions.trap: A neutrino goes with β⁺ (positron) decay.

questions.q: ²³⁸U (Z = 92) decays into ²⁰⁶Pb (Z = 82). The numbers of α and β⁻ particles emitted are
questions.x: α count = (238 − 206)/4 = 8, lowering Z by 16 to 76. To reach 82, six β⁻ decays (each Z + 1) are needed.

questions.q: The mean life of a radioactive substance with a half-life of 6.93 days is
questions.x: τ = T½/0.693 = 6.93/0.693 = 10 days. Mean life is always 1.44 times the half-life.
questions.trap: 4.8 days multiplies by 0.693 instead of dividing.

questions.q: The SI unit of radioactivity is the
questions.x: 1 Bq = 1 disintegration per second. The curie (3.7 × 10¹⁰ Bq) is an older unit; gray and sievert measure dose.

questions.q: The fraction of a radioactive sample that has decayed after 4 half-lives is
questions.x: Remaining = (½)⁴ = 1/16, so decayed = 1 − 1/16 = 15/16.
questions.trap: 1/16 is the fraction remaining, not decayed.

questions.q: The activity of a sample falls from 800 to 100 counts per second in 30 minutes. Its half-life is
questions.x: 800 → 400 → 200 → 100 is 3 half-lives in 30 min, so T½ = 10 min.
questions.trap: 3.75 min divides 30 by the ratio 8 instead of by 3 halvings.

questions.q: Radiocarbon dating of ancient wood uses the isotope
questions.x: Living things keep a fixed C-14/C-12 ratio; after death C-14 decays (T½ ≈ 5730 years), and the remaining fraction gives the age.

questions.q: An ancient wooden sample shows one-quarter of the C-14 activity of fresh wood. Taking T½ = 5730 years, its age is about
questions.x: 1/4 = (½)², i.e. 2 half-lives = 2 × 5730 = 11460 years.
questions.trap: 22920 years uses 4 half-lives instead of 2.

questions.q: Cobalt-60 is used in medicine mainly as a source of
questions.x: Co-60 emits penetrating γ-rays used to destroy tumour cells. I-131 is used for thyroid disorders.

questions.q: The SI unit of equivalent dose, which accounts for the biological effect of radiation, is the
questions.x: Gray (J kg⁻¹) measures absorbed dose; multiplying by a radiation weighting factor gives equivalent dose in sieverts.
questions.trap: Gray is absorbed dose, without the biological weighting.

questions.q: The rate of decay of a radioactive sample depends on
o: The number of undecayed nuclei present
The chemical compound it is in
questions.x: dN/dt = −λN. Decay is a nuclear process, unaffected by temperature, pressure or chemical state.

questions.q: The correct order of forbidden energy gap is
questions.x: Insulators have a wide gap (over about 3 eV), semiconductors a small gap (Si 1.1 eV), and in conductors the bands overlap (gap ≈ 0).

questions.q: The forbidden energy gap of silicon at room temperature is about
questions.x: Si ≈ 1.1 eV and Ge ≈ 0.7 eV. About 6 eV is typical of an insulator such as diamond.

questions.q: To make germanium a p-type semiconductor, it should be doped with
questions.x: Trivalent impurities (B, Al, Ga, In) accept electrons, creating holes. As, Sb and P are pentavalent donors that make n-type.
questions.trap: Arsenic, antimony and phosphorus give n-type, not p-type.

questions.q: A p-type semiconductor, taken as a whole, is
questions.x: Each acceptor atom is itself neutral; the hole and the ionised acceptor balance. Holes are majority carriers, but net charge is zero.
questions.trap: Majority holes do not make the crystal positively charged.

questions.q: At absolute zero, a pure (intrinsic) semiconductor behaves as
questions.x: At 0 K no electrons have enough energy to cross the gap; the conduction band is empty, so it cannot conduct.

questions.q: In an intrinsic semiconductor, the number of free electrons n_e and holes n_h are related by
questions.x: Each electron that crosses the gap leaves exactly one hole behind, so they are created in equal numbers.

questions.q: The potential barrier across a p-n junction is due to
o: Immobile ionised donors and acceptors in the depletion layer
Free electrons collecting on the p-side
questions.x: Diffusion of majority carriers across the junction leaves fixed positive donor ions on the n-side and negative acceptor ions on the p-side.
questions.trap: The barrier exists even with no battery connected.

questions.q: The barrier potential of a silicon p-n junction diode is about
questions.x: Silicon about 0.7 V; germanium about 0.3 V.
questions.trap: 0.3 V is the germanium value.

questions.q: When a p-n junction is forward biased, the depletion layer
questions.x: The applied voltage opposes the barrier, pushing carriers towards the junction and narrowing the depletion region. Reverse bias widens it.

questions.q: A p-n junction diode is forward biased when
o: The p-side is connected to the positive terminal of the battery
The n-side is connected to the positive terminal
The p-side is connected to the negative terminal
questions.x: Positive to p and negative to n lowers the barrier and lets majority carriers cross the junction.

questions.q: The small current through a reverse-biased p-n junction is due to
questions.x: Reverse bias blocks majority carriers; thermally generated minority carriers drift across, giving a tiny saturation current.
questions.trap: Ions in the depletion layer are fixed and carry no current.

questions.q: A half-wave rectifier is fed with 50 Hz AC. The frequency of the output pulses is
questions.x: Only one half of each cycle passes, so there is one pulse per input cycle: 50 Hz. A full-wave rectifier gives 100 Hz.
questions.trap: 100 Hz is the full-wave value.

questions.q: Which logic gate can be used on its own to build every other logic gate?
questions.x: NAND (and NOR) are universal gates: NOT, AND and OR can all be made by connecting NAND gates.

questions.q: Which pair are known as universal gates?
questions.x: Any Boolean function can be built from only NAND gates, or from only NOR gates.

questions.q: A two-input gate gives output 0 only when both inputs are 1. The gate is
questions.x: NAND truth table: 00 → 1, 01 → 1, 10 → 1, 11 → 0. It is AND followed by NOT.
questions.trap: AND gives 1, not 0, when both inputs are 1.

questions.q: The output of an OR gate is fed into a NOT gate. The combination acts as a
questions.x: NOT(A + B) is the NOR function by definition.
questions.trap: NAND is AND followed by NOT.

questions.q: The Boolean expression for an OR gate with inputs A and B is
questions.x: OR gives 1 when at least one input is 1: Y = A + B. A · B is AND; the complement of A + B is NOR.

questions.q: A NOT gate with input A = 1 gives the output
questions.x: A NOT gate inverts: Y = Ā, so 1 → 0 and 0 → 1.

questions.q: The quark composition of a proton is
questions.x: Proton = up + up + down: charge 2/3 + 2/3 − 1/3 = +1. Neutron = udd.
questions.trap: udd is the neutron.

questions.q: The quark composition of a neutron is
questions.x: Neutron = up + down + down: 2/3 − 1/3 − 1/3 = 0.

questions.q: Which of the following particles contains no quarks?
questions.x: Antineutrinos are leptons, which are fundamental and have no quark content. Protons and neutrons are three-quark baryons; pions are quark–antiquark mesons.
questions.trap: Pions are mesons, built from a quark and an antiquark.

questions.q: The charge on an up quark is
questions.x: Up quark +2/3 e, down quark −1/3 e. Quarks carry fractional charges but are never seen alone.

questions.q: The antiparticle of the electron is the
questions.x: The positron has the same mass as the electron but charge +e.

questions.q: Leptons such as the electron, muon and neutrinos are particles that
o: Do not feel the strong nuclear force
Feel only the strong nuclear force
questions.x: Leptons are fundamental and take part only in weak (and, if charged, electromagnetic) interactions. Hadrons feel the strong force.

questions.q: The Higgs boson, discovered at CERN in 2012, is linked to
o: The mechanism that gives fundamental particles their mass
questions.x: Particles gain mass by interacting with the Higgs field; the Higgs boson is that field's quantum. Gluons bind quarks.

questions.q: Hubble's law states that the speed at which a distant galaxy recedes from us is
o: Proportional to the square of its distance
questions.x: v = H₀d: farther galaxies recede faster, showing that the universe is expanding.

questions.q: A galaxy recedes at 1400 km s⁻¹. If the Hubble constant is 70 km s⁻¹ Mpc⁻¹, its distance is
questions.trap: 98000 Mpc multiplies v by H₀ instead of dividing.

questions.q: The reciprocal of the Hubble constant (1/H₀) gives an estimate of the
questions.x: If galaxies have receded at constant speed, d = vt and v = H₀d give t = 1/H₀ ≈ 14 billion years (the Hubble time).

questions.q: The existence of dark matter is inferred mainly from
o: Its gravitational effects, such as the rotation speeds of galaxies
questions.x: Dark matter neither emits nor absorbs light; outer stars orbit galaxies too fast for visible mass alone, revealing extra unseen mass.

questions.q: Strong evidence for the Big Bang theory is the
o: Cosmic microwave background radiation at about 2.7 K
questions.x: The CMB is the cooled afterglow of the hot early universe; with galactic redshift it supports the Big Bang.

questions.q: The redshift of light from distant galaxies indicates that
o: The galaxies are moving away from us
The galaxies are moving towards us
questions.x: A shift to longer wavelengths (Doppler) means recession. Blueshift would mean approach.

questions.q: Nanotechnology deals with structures having sizes of roughly
questions.x: 1 nm = 10⁻⁹ m. At 1–100 nm, materials show new properties due to quantum and surface effects.

questions.q: Nanoparticles often behave differently from the bulk material mainly because they have a
o: Very large surface area to volume ratio
questions.x: Shrinking size raises the fraction of atoms at the surface, changing reactivity, optical and electrical properties.

questions.q: An electron and a positron at rest annihilate each other. The result is
o: Two γ-ray photons of about 0.511 MeV each
questions.x: Total rest energy 2 × 0.511 MeV appears as two photons moving in opposite directions, conserving momentum.
questions.trap: A single photon cannot conserve momentum when the pair starts at rest.

questions.q: A metal wire has a resistance of 5 Ω at 0 °C and a temperature coefficient of resistance of 0.004 °C⁻¹. Its resistance at 50 °C is
questions.x: R_t = R₀(1 + αt) = 5(1 + 0.004 × 50) = 5 × 1.2 = 6 Ω. A metal's resistance rises with temperature.
questions.trap: 4 Ω: subtracting, as if metal resistance fell on heating like a semiconductor's.

questions.q: The capacitance of a parallel plate capacitor does NOT depend on
o: The metal the plates are made of
questions.x: C = Kε₀A/d depends only on geometry (A, d) and the medium (K). Any conducting metal gives the same C.

questions.q: A uniform magnetic field of 0.2 T passes through a coil of area 50 cm², making 60° with the normal to the coil. The magnetic flux through the coil is
questions.trap: 1 × 10⁻³ Wb ignores the angle; 10 Wb forgets cm² → m².

questions.q: A 10 V battery is connected through a switch to a coil of inductance 2 H and resistance 5 Ω. Just after the switch is closed, the current is
questions.x: The self-induced emf opposes the sudden rise, so the current starts at zero and grows as I = (E/R)(1 − e^(−Rt/L)) towards E/R = 2 A.
questions.trap: 2 A is the final steady current, reached only after a long time.

questions.s: Electric field strength, potential and potential energy
questions.q: Moving a charge of 4 C between two points needs 20 J of work. The potential difference between the points is
questions.x: Potential difference is work per unit charge: V = W/q = 20/4 = 5 V.
questions.trap: 80 V multiplies instead of dividing.

questions.q: A particle of rest mass m₀ moves at 0.6c. According to special relativity, its mass is
questions.x: m = m₀/√(1 − v²/c²) = m₀/√(1 − 0.36) = m₀/0.8 = 1.25 m₀. Mass increases with speed.
questions.trap: 0.8 m₀ multiplies by √(1 − v²/c²) instead of dividing.

questions.q: In β⁺ (positron) decay, the daughter nucleus has
o: The same mass number and atomic number one more
The same mass number and atomic number one less
Mass number one less and the same atomic number
The same mass number and the same atomic number
questions.x: A proton turns into a neutron, emitting a positron and a neutrino: A is unchanged, Z falls by 1.
questions.trap: Z + 1 is β⁻ decay, where a neutron becomes a proton.

questions.q: In a nuclear reactor, fission of a ²³⁵U nucleus is started by the absorption of a
questions.x: The uncharged neutron is not repelled by the nucleus; ²³⁵U captures slow neutrons most readily, forming unstable ²³⁶U that splits.
questions.trap: Protons are repelled by the nucleus's positive charge.

questions.q: The fundamental forces of nature are transmitted by the exchange of particles called
questions.x: Force carriers are bosons: photon (electromagnetic), gluons (strong), W and Z (weak), and the hypothetical graviton. Fermions (quarks, leptons) make up matter.
questions.trap: Fermions build matter; they do not carry forces.

questions.q: X-rays of wavelength λ fall on a crystal whose atomic planes are a distance d apart. Bragg reflection can occur only if
questions.x: 2d sin θ = nλ with sin θ ≤ 1 needs nλ ≤ 2d; the first order needs λ ≤ 2d. This is why X-rays, not visible light, are diffracted by crystals.

questions.q: An electron (e/m = 1.76 × 10¹¹ C kg⁻¹) is placed in a uniform electric field of 100 V m⁻¹. The magnitude of its acceleration is
questions.trap: 1.76 × 10⁹ divides by E instead of multiplying.

questions.q: A Zener diode used as a voltage regulator is operated in the
questions.x: A heavily doped Zener diode breaks down at a sharp, fixed reverse voltage; the voltage across it then stays almost constant over a wide current range.

questions.q: In the hydrogen spectrum, the ratio of the wavelength of the photon emitted in the n = 3 → 2 transition to that emitted in the n = 2 → 1 transition is
questions.trap: 5 : 27 is the ratio of energies, not wavelengths.

questions.q: Identical capacitors of 4 μF, each able to withstand 200 V, are to be combined to give 4 μF that can withstand 600 V. The least number needed is
questions.x: 600 V needs 3 in series per row (4/3 μF per row). Rows in parallel to reach 4 μF: 4 ÷ (4/3) = 3. Total 3 × 3 = 9.
questions.trap: 3 meets the voltage but gives only 4/3 μF.

questions.q: A 220 V house circuit is protected by a 5 A fuse. The largest number of 100 W, 220 V bulbs that can be run together in parallel is
questions.x: Maximum power = VI = 220 × 5 = 1100 W. 1100/100 = 11 bulbs.
questions.trap: 5: taking the fuse rating in amperes as the number of bulbs.

questions.q: An electron moves towards the east in a uniform magnetic field directed vertically upward. The magnetic force on it is towards the
questions.x: F = q(v × B). For a positive charge, east × up = south. The electron is negative, so the force is reversed: north.
questions.trap: South: forgetting the electron's negative charge.

questions.q: A nucleus at rest emits an α-particle. Compared with the α-particle, the recoiling daughter nucleus has
o: Equal kinetic energy but less momentum
More momentum and more kinetic energy
Equal momentum but much less kinetic energy
questions.x: Momentum conservation: the two move apart with equal and opposite momenta. KE = p²/2m, so the heavier daughter gets far less KE; the α carries most of the energy.
questions.trap: Equal KE: momentum, not KE, is shared equally.

questions.q: In Millikan's oil drop experiment, a charged drop stays stationary between the plates when
o: The magnetic force on it balances its weight
The electric force on it balances its weight
The air pressure above and below it is equal
questions.x: With the drop at rest (no viscous drag), qE = mg. Knowing E and m gives q, which always came out as a whole multiple of e.

questions.q: A charged oil drop is held stationary by a vertical electric field. If the direction of the field is suddenly reversed, the initial acceleration of the drop is
questions.x: Before: qE upward = mg. After reversal, qE acts downward too, so net force = 2mg downward and a = 2g (drag is zero at the start).
questions.trap: g ignores that the electric force now adds to the weight.

questions.q: An electron moves at 1.76 × 10⁶ m s⁻¹ at right angles to a uniform magnetic field of 1 × 10⁻³ T. The radius of its circular path is (e/m = 1.76 × 10¹¹ C kg⁻¹)
An electron starts from rest and is accelerated through a potential difference of 100 V. Its final speed is about (e/m = 1.76 × 10¹¹ C kg⁻¹)
questions.trap: 3.5 × 10¹³ forgets to take the square root.

questions.q: J.J. Thomson found that the specific charge (e/m) of cathode-ray particles
o: Depends on the gas in the tube
Depends on the metal of the cathode
Is the same whatever gas or cathode metal is used
Is equal to that of the hydrogen ion
questions.x: The same e/m from every gas and cathode showed that these particles (electrons) are a common constituent of all atoms.

questions.q: Compared with the specific charge of an electron, the specific charge of a proton is
questions.x: Both carry charge of magnitude e, but m_p ≈ 1836 m_e. So e/m_p is about 1836 times smaller than e/m_e.
questions.trap: 1836 times reverses the ratio: the lighter electron has the larger e/m.

questions.q: An electron enters the space between two charged parallel plates moving parallel to the plates. While between the plates, its velocity component parallel to the plates
questions.x: The electric force is perpendicular to the plates, so there is no acceleration along them. Only the perpendicular component changes, giving a parabolic path.

questions.q: An electron enters a uniform magnetic field with its velocity at 30° to the field direction. Its path in the field is a
questions.x: The component v cos 30° along B is unaffected; the component v sin 30° makes it circle about B. Together they give a helix.
questions.trap: Circle only when the velocity is exactly perpendicular to B.

questions.q: Taking R = R₀A^(1/3) with R₀ = 1.2 fm, the radius of a nucleus of mass number 125 is
questions.trap: 150 fm multiplies by A instead of A^(1/3).

questions.q: Nuclei having the same number of neutrons but different numbers of protons are called
questions.x: Isotopes: same Z. Isobars: same A. Isotones: same neutron number N = A − Z.

questions.q: The number of neutrons in a nucleus of ²³⁵₉₂U is
The binding energy of the ⁴₂He nucleus is about 28 MeV. Its binding energy per nucleon is about
questions.x: Divide by the number of nucleons A = 4: 28/4 = 7 MeV.
questions.trap: 14 MeV divides by the number of protons instead of nucleons.

questions.q: Taking m_p = 1.00728 u, m_n = 1.00867 u, the mass of a deuteron = 2.01355 u and 1 u = 931.5 MeV, the binding energy of the deuteron is about
questions.trap: 1.1 MeV is the binding energy per nucleon, not the total.

questions.q: Per kilogram of fuel, compared with nuclear fission, nuclear fusion of light nuclei releases
questions.x: Fission of ²³⁵U gives about 0.85 MeV per nucleon; fusion of hydrogen isotopes gives several MeV per nucleon, so fusion yields more per unit mass.
questions.trap: Per reaction fission gives more (≈200 MeV), but per unit mass fusion wins.

questions.q: Energy is released when a heavy nucleus such as ²³⁵U undergoes fission because the fragments
o: Have a higher binding energy per nucleon
Have a lower binding energy per nucleon
questions.x: BE per nucleon is about 7.6 MeV for uranium but about 8.5 MeV for mid-mass fragments. The products are more tightly bound, so their total mass is smaller and the difference appears as energy.

questions.q: In a thermal nuclear reactor, the moderator (such as heavy water or graphite) is used to
questions.x: Fission neutrons are fast; ²³⁵U captures slow (thermal) neutrons far better. Light nuclei in the moderator take energy from neutrons by collisions.
questions.trap: Absorbing neutrons is the job of the cadmium or boron control rods.

questions.q: A nuclear chain reaction proceeds at a steady rate (critical condition) when the neutron multiplication factor k is
questions.x: k = 1: each fission causes on average one more fission, as in a working reactor. k > 1 grows rapidly (bomb); k < 1 dies out.

questions.q: The momentum of a photon of wavelength λ is
questions.x: p = E/c = hν/c = h/λ. hc/λ is the photon's energy, not its momentum.
questions.trap: hc/λ is the energy of the photon.

questions.q: Very intense light of frequency below the threshold frequency falls on a metal surface. Photoelectrons are
questions.x: Each photon hν is less than the work function, and one electron absorbs one photon. More photons (intensity) cannot add up their energies.

questions.q: The work function of a metal is 4.14 eV. Its threshold frequency is about (h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s, 1 eV = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ J)
The time lag between light falling on a photosensitive surface and the emission of photoelectrons is
questions.x: Emission is instantaneous because an electron absorbs a whole photon at once. Wave theory wrongly predicted a delay for faint light.
questions.trap: A delay for faint light is the wave-theory prediction, disproved by experiment.

questions.q: Light of frequency 2ν₀ and then light of frequency 5ν₀ falls on a metal of threshold frequency ν₀. The ratio of the maximum speeds of the photoelectrons in the two cases is
questions.x: KE_max = h(ν − ν₀): hν₀ and 4hν₀, ratio 1 : 4. Speed ∝ √KE, so the speed ratio is 1 : 2.
questions.trap: 1 : 4 is the ratio of kinetic energies, not speeds.

questions.q: On the graph of stopping potential against frequency of incident light, the intercept on the frequency axis gives the
questions.x: eV₀ = hν − φ. V₀ = 0 when ν = ν₀, so the line cuts the frequency axis at the threshold frequency. The slope is h/e.
questions.trap: Planck's constant comes from the slope, not the intercept.

questions.q: Einstein's photoelectric equation is (φ = work function)
questions.x: The photon energy is used to free the electron (φ) and the rest appears as its maximum kinetic energy.

questions.q: Photocells used in automatic doors and burglar alarms work on the
questions.x: Light falling on the cathode releases electrons and a current flows; interrupting the light beam stops the current and operates a relay.

questions.q: A metal has a work function of 2.5 eV. To get photoelectrons with a stopping potential of 1.5 V, the wavelength of light needed is (hc = 12400 eV Å)
questions.x: Photon energy = φ + eV₀ = 2.5 + 1.5 = 4 eV. λ = 12400/4 = 3100 Å.
questions.trap: 4960 Å uses only the work function.

questions.q: If the kinetic energy of a free electron becomes 4 times, its de Broglie wavelength becomes
questions.x: λ = h/p = h/√(2mK), so λ ∝ 1/√K. Four times K gives λ/2.
questions.trap: One-fourth treats λ as ∝ 1/K instead of 1/√K.

questions.q: The shortest wavelength in the Lyman series of hydrogen is about (R = 1.097 × 10⁷ m⁻¹)
questions.x: Series limit: n₂ = ∞ → 1, so 1/λ = R(1/1² − 0) and λ = 1/R ≈ 9.12 × 10⁻⁸ m = 912 Å.
questions.trap: 1216 Å is the longest Lyman line (2 → 1).

questions.q: The total energy of the electron in a Bohr orbit of hydrogen is −3.4 eV. Its kinetic energy in that orbit is
questions.x: In a Bohr orbit KE = −E and PE = 2E. So KE = +3.4 eV and PE = −6.8 eV.
questions.trap: −6.8 eV is the potential energy.

questions.q: The characteristic (line) X-ray spectrum of a target is produced when
o: Fast electrons are slowed down by nuclei
Electrons jump between inner shells of the target atoms
Valence electrons of the target are excited
questions.x: An incoming electron knocks out an inner (e.g. K-shell) electron; an outer electron drops into the vacancy, emitting X-rays at wavelengths fixed by the element.
questions.trap: Slowing down by nuclei gives the continuous (bremsstrahlung) spectrum.

questions.q: The half-life of a radioactive isotope is 693 s. Its decay constant is
The correct order of penetrating power of radioactive radiations is
questions.x: Penetrating power is the reverse of ionising power: α is stopped by paper, β by a few mm of aluminium, γ needs thick lead.
questions.trap: α > β > γ is the order of ionising power.

questions.q: A nucleus emits one α-particle and then two β⁻ particles. The final nucleus is
o: An isobar of the original nucleus
An isotone of the original nucleus
An isotope of the original nucleus
The same nuclide as the original
questions.x: α: A − 4, Z − 2. Two β⁻: Z + 2, A unchanged. Net: A − 4, Z unchanged, so it is an isotope of the parent.

questions.q: One curie (1 Ci), an older unit of activity, equals
questions.x: 1 Ci = 3.7 × 10¹⁰ disintegrations per second, roughly the activity of 1 g of radium. 1 Bq = 1 decay per second.

questions.q: Taken into the body (for example by inhaling radon), the radiation that is most harmful to tissue is
questions.x: Inside the body, α-particles deposit all their energy in a tiny volume of tissue because their ionising power is highest. Outside, skin stops them.
questions.trap: γ is the most penetrating, which matters for sources outside the body.

questions.q: Two radioactive samples X and Y start with equal numbers of nuclei. Their half-lives are 1 h and 2 h. After 4 h, the ratio of undecayed nuclei X : Y is
questions.x: X: 4 half-lives → N₀/16. Y: 2 half-lives → N₀/4. Ratio (1/16) : (1/4) = 1 : 4.
questions.trap: 1 : 2 uses the ratio of half-lives directly.

questions.q: Arsenic (pentavalent) added to pure silicon acts as a
o: Acceptor impurity, giving a p-type semiconductor
Donor impurity, giving a p-type semiconductor
Donor impurity, giving an n-type semiconductor
Acceptor impurity, giving an n-type semiconductor
questions.x: Four of arsenic's five valence electrons bond with Si; the fifth is donated as a free electron, so electrons are the majority carriers.

questions.q: A two-input AND gate has inputs A = 1 and B = 0. Its output is
questions.x: AND gives 1 only when all inputs are 1 (Y = A·B = 1·0 = 0).

questions.q: In a metallic conductor, the valence band and the conduction band
o: Are separated by more than 3 eV
questions.x: With no forbidden gap, electrons move freely into empty states, so metals conduct at all temperatures. Semiconductors have a small gap, insulators a large one.

questions.q: When the reverse bias across a p-n junction is increased (below breakdown), the depletion layer
o: Becomes thinner and the barrier falls
Becomes wider and the barrier rises
questions.x: Reverse bias pulls majority carriers away from the junction, exposing more immobile ions. The depletion layer widens and the potential barrier increases.
questions.trap: Thinner is what forward bias does.

questions.q: Both inputs of a NAND gate are joined together and fed with a single input A. The gate now works as a
questions.x: Y = (A·A)′ = A′. Input 0 gives 1, input 1 gives 0, which is an inverter.

questions.q: In a full-wave bridge rectifier, the number of diodes that conduct during each half-cycle of the input is
questions.x: Of the four diodes, one opposite pair conducts in one half-cycle and the other pair in the next, so current flows the same way through the load each time.
questions.trap: 4 is the total number of diodes, not those conducting at once.

questions.q: Which of these particles is a lepton?
questions.x: Leptons (electron, muon, tau and their neutrinos) are fundamental and contain no quarks. Protons and neutrons are baryons; pions are mesons.

questions.q: A baryon made of the quarks u, u and s has a charge of (u = +2/3 e, s = −1/3 e)
questions.x: Charge = 2/3 + 2/3 − 1/3 = +1 e. The strange quark has the same charge as the down quark.

questions.q: Two galaxies are 50 Mpc and 150 Mpc away from us. By Hubble's law, the ratio of their recession speeds is
A thermocouple converts
o: Heat energy directly into electrical energy
questions.x: Keeping the two junctions of dissimilar metals at different temperatures produces a thermo-emf (Seebeck effect).

questions.q: As the hot junction of a thermocouple is heated, the thermo-emf is maximum at the
questions.x: The emf rises with temperature to a maximum at the neutral temperature, then falls, and reverses direction at the temperature of inversion.
questions.trap: At inversion the emf is zero, not maximum.

questions.q: The neutral temperature of a thermocouple
o: Is the same for every pair of metals
Depends only on the two metals, not on the cold-junction temperature
questions.x: θn is fixed for a given pair of metals. The inversion temperature θi = 2θn − θc does depend on the cold junction.
questions.trap: The inversion temperature, not the neutral one, shifts with the cold junction.

questions.q: The thermo-emf of a thermocouple is E = (40θ − 0.04θ²) μV, where θ is the hot-junction temperature in °C with the cold junction at 0 °C. Its neutral temperature is
questions.x: At the neutral temperature dE/dθ = 0: 40 − 0.08θ = 0, so θ = 500 °C. (E = 0 again at 1000 °C, the inversion temperature.)
questions.trap: 1000 °C is where E becomes zero: the inversion temperature.

questions.q: The relative permeability of a diamagnetic substance is
questions.x: μr = 1 + χ and χ is small and negative for diamagnetic materials, so μr is just below 1.

questions.q: Magnetic domains, small regions in which atomic magnetic moments are all aligned, exist in
questions.x: Domains explain the strong magnetisation of iron, cobalt and nickel. An applied field grows favourably aligned domains.

questions.q: A material has magnetic susceptibility 999. Its relative permeability is
A small piece of a paramagnetic substance is placed in a non-uniform magnetic field. It
o: Moves strongly from the stronger to the weaker part
Moves weakly from the stronger to the weaker part
Moves weakly from the weaker to the stronger part of the field
questions.x: Paramagnets are weakly magnetised along the field and are drawn towards stronger field. Diamagnets are pushed towards weaker field.
questions.trap: Moving to the weaker region is diamagnetic behaviour.

questions.q: The magnetic susceptibility of which type of material is almost independent of temperature?
questions.x: Diamagnetism comes from induced orbital currents, which do not depend on thermal agitation. Paramagnetic χ ∝ 1/T; ferromagnetism vanishes above the Curie temperature.

questions.q: A paramagnetic salt has susceptibility 1.2 × 10⁻⁵ at 300 K. Its susceptibility at 200 K is
questions.trap: 0.8 × 10⁻⁵ takes χ ∝ T.

questions.q: On a hysteresis loop, the reverse magnetising field needed to bring the magnetisation of a material to zero is called its
questions.x: Retentivity is the magnetisation left when H = 0; coercivity is the reverse H needed to remove it.
questions.trap: Retentivity is the leftover magnetisation, not the field needed to remove it.

questions.q: If the frequency of an AC supply is doubled, the reactance of a capacitor connected to it
questions.x: X_C = 1/(2πfC), so X_C ∝ 1/f. An inductor behaves the opposite way: X_L = 2πfL.
questions.trap: Doubling describes an inductor's reactance.

questions.q: A series circuit has R = 8 Ω, X_L = 10 Ω and X_C = 4 Ω. Its impedance is
questions.trap: 22 Ω simply adds all three.

questions.q: In a series LC circuit, both L and C are doubled. The resonant frequency becomes
questions.x: f₀ = 1/(2π√(LC)). LC becomes 4 times, √(LC) doubles, so f₀ halves.
questions.trap: One-fourth forgets the square root.

questions.q: An AC voltmeter reads 100 V. The peak value of the voltage is about
questions.x: AC meters read rms values. V₀ = √2 × V_rms = 1.414 × 100 ≈ 141 V.
questions.trap: 70.7 V divides by √2 instead of multiplying.

questions.q: At resonance in a series LCR circuit, the power factor is
o: 1, as current and voltage are in phase
questions.x: At resonance X_L = X_C, so Z = R and the phase angle is zero. Power factor cos φ = R/Z = 1.

questions.q: An AC circuit has V_rms = 200 V and I_rms = 5 A, with the current lagging the voltage by 60°. The average power consumed is
questions.x: P = V_rms I_rms cos φ = 200 × 5 × cos 60° = 500 W.
questions.trap: 1000 W ignores the power factor.

questions.q: The magnetic field lines around a long straight current-carrying wire are
o: Concentric circles centred on the wire
Straight lines parallel to the wire
Straight lines radiating from the wire
questions.x: The lines circle the wire in planes perpendicular to it; their direction is given by the right-hand grip rule.

questions.q: A circular coil of 100 turns and radius 10 cm carries a current of 1 A. The magnetic field at its centre is (μ₀ = 4π × 10⁻⁷ T m A⁻¹)
questions.trap: 1.26 × 10⁻³ T forgets the 2 in 2r.

questions.q: A 0.5 m wire carrying 4 A lies at 30° to a uniform magnetic field of 0.2 T. The magnetic force on it is
questions.trap: 0.4 N ignores the angle.

questions.q: A proton and a deuteron (same charge, twice the mass) enter a uniform magnetic field at right angles with the same kinetic energy. The ratio of the radii of their paths r_p : r_d is
questions.x: r = mv/qB = √(2mK)/qB. Same K and q, so r ∝ √m: r_p : r_d = 1 : √2.
questions.trap: 1 : 2 holds for equal speeds, not equal kinetic energies.

questions.q: A long solenoid has 1000 turns per metre and carries 2 A. The magnetic field inside it is about (μ₀ = 4π × 10⁻⁷ T m A⁻¹)
Two long parallel wires 1 m apart in vacuum each carry a current of 1 A. The force per metre between them is
questions.x: F/L = μ₀I₁I₂/(2πd) = 4π × 10⁻⁷ × 1 × 1/(2π × 1) = 2 × 10⁻⁷ N. This was the old definition of the ampere.
questions.trap: 4π × 10⁻⁷ is μ₀ itself, not the force.

questions.q: The north pole of a bar magnet is pushed towards a coil. The face of the coil nearer the magnet behaves as a
o: North pole only after the magnet stops
questions.x: By Lenz's law the induced current opposes the approach, so the near face becomes a north pole and repels the magnet.
questions.trap: South pole would attract the magnet and break energy conservation.

questions.q: Eddy currents are put to useful work in
questions.x: Eddy currents oppose motion (braking) and heat metal (induction furnace). Laminating a core is done to reduce them, not to use them.
questions.trap: Laminations exist to reduce eddy currents.

questions.q: A 0.5 m rod moves at 4 m s⁻¹ at right angles to a uniform magnetic field of 0.2 T, with the rod, its velocity and the field mutually perpendicular. The emf induced across its ends is
questions.x: Motional emf e = Blv = 0.2 × 0.5 × 4 = 0.4 V.

questions.q: The mutual inductance of two coils is 0.2 H. If the current in one coil changes steadily by 5 A in 0.1 s, the emf induced in the other is
questions.trap: 1 V forgets to divide by the time.

questions.q: A long solenoid has its number of turns doubled, keeping its length and area the same. Its self-inductance becomes
questions.x: L = μ₀N²A/l, so L ∝ N². Doubling N makes L four times.
questions.trap: Twice forgets that N enters squared.

questions.q: To double the energy stored in an inductor, the current through it must be multiplied by
questions.x: U = ½LI², so U ∝ I². Doubling U needs I multiplied by √2.
questions.trap: 2 would make the energy four times.

questions.q: Ten identical resistors are first joined in series and then in parallel. The ratio R_series : R_parallel is
questions.x: Series: 10R. Parallel: R/10. Ratio = 10R ÷ (R/10) = 100.
questions.trap: 10 : 1 compares only one of the two arrangements with a single resistor.

questions.q: At a junction, currents of 3 A and 2 A flow in and 4 A flows out along a third wire. The current in the fourth wire is
questions.x: Kirchhoff's junction law: total in = total out. 3 + 2 = 4 + I, so I = 1 A outward.

questions.q: The sensitivity of a potentiometer can be increased by
o: Decreasing the length of the wire
Using a wire of higher resistance per cm, with the same current
Increasing the length of the wire, keeping the same driving cell
Increasing the current in the wire
questions.x: A longer wire lowers the potential gradient (V per cm), so a small emf difference gives a larger shift in balancing length.
questions.trap: More current raises the potential gradient and lowers sensitivity.

questions.q: On a potentiometer, a cell balances at 100 cm on open circuit. When a 4 Ω resistor is joined across the cell, the balance point moves to 80 cm. The internal resistance of the cell is
A galvanometer is converted into an ammeter with a shunt of resistance S. The resistance of the resulting ammeter is
questions.x: The shunt and the galvanometer are in parallel, and a parallel combination is smaller than its smallest branch, so R_A < S.

questions.q: A copper wire of length L and diameter d has resistance R. A copper wire of length 2L and diameter 2d has resistance
questions.x: R = ρL/A with A ∝ d². Length ×2 doubles R; diameter ×2 makes area ×4, dividing R by 4. Net: R × 2/4 = R/2.
questions.trap: R forgets that area goes as diameter squared.
